cards.front: Inside an ecosystem, decomposers release an element and plants take it up again. Why can that loop be larger than all the inputs and still not change the ecosystem's store?
cards.back: The loop only moves atoms between pools inside the boundary, so each release is matched by uptake and it cancels in the sum. Only fluxes that cross the boundary change the store.
cards.quote: That loop can be several times larger than all the inputs, yet it cancels in the sum.

cards.front: A {{c1::pool}} (or stock) is the amount of an element in one compartment at one time, in mass per area (kg N per hectare).
cards.quote: A pool (or stock) is the amount of an element in one compartment at one time, in mass per area (kg N per hectare).
cards.section: Pools, fluxes and residence time

cards.front: In an ecosystem nutrient budget, what is a flux, and what are its units?
cards.back: A transfer between pools, or across the boundary, in mass per area per time (for example kg N per hectare per year).
cards.quote: A flux is a transfer between pools, or across the boundary (the line that decides what counts as inside), in mass per area per time
cards.section: Pools, fluxes and residence time

cards.front: For a stated boundary and interval, change in stock = {{c1::inputs − outputs}}.
cards.back: Internal transfers do not appear; only boundary fluxes count.
cards.quote: change in stock = inputs − outputs (for a stated boundary and interval)
cards.section: Pools, fluxes and residence time

cards.front: What is residence time, and how is it calculated?
cards.back: The average time an atom spends in a pool when inflow and outflow balance: residence time = stock / flux through the pool.
cards.quote: Residence time is the average time an atom spends in a pool when inflow and outflow balance.
cards.section: Pools, fluxes and residence time

cards.front: A nutrient budget is a mass balance like the one used for energy flow. What is the key difference between the two?
cards.back: Energy leaves an ecosystem as heat and is not reused, while atoms of an element are reused again and again.
cards.quote: This is the mass balance from energy flow, except that energy leaves as heat while atoms are reused.
cards.section: Pools, fluxes and residence time

cards.front: An invented watershed (boundary from canopy to bedrock) receives 7 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ in deposition and 4 from fixation. Stream export is 2 and denitrification is 3, same units. What is the change in the watershed's nitrogen stock?
cards.back: Inputs 7 + 4 = 11; outputs 2 + 3 = 5; change = 11 − 5 = +6 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹, a net gain stored inside.
cards.why: change in stock = inputs − outputs; internal cycling does not enter the sum.
cards.quote: inputs 14; outputs 3 by the stream and 2 by denitrification
cards.section: Pools, fluxes and residence time

cards.front: A forest soil holds 2,400 kg organic N per hectare, and gross mineralisation releases 80 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ from it. Assuming the pool is near balance, what is the residence time of nitrogen in soil organic matter?
cards.back: Residence time = stock / flux = 2,400 / 80 = 30 years, the average wait before decomposers release an atom.
cards.why: Valid only if inflow and outflow of the pool roughly balance; otherwise it is an estimate.
cards.quote: Residence time = 4,500 / 90 = 50 years, the average wait before decomposers release an atom.
cards.section: Pools, fluxes and residence time

cards.front: A watershed has inputs of 14 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ and denitrification of 2. After the forest is cut and regrowth suppressed, stream export rises to 30 while the other terms are assumed fixed. What is the change in stock?
cards.back: Outputs = 30 + 2 = 32; change = 14 − 32 = −18 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹, a net loss.
cards.why: Assuming the other terms stay fixed; gas losses could rise too.
cards.quote: Suppose stream export rises to 40 while the other terms stay fixed (an assumption; gas losses could rise too).
cards.section: Pools, fluxes and residence time

cards.front: In the Hubbard Brook small-watershed approach, why choose valleys on watertight bedrock with a weir at the outlet?
cards.back: Little water seeps deep, so the weir, which gauges stream flow, measures nearly everything leaving in liquid water, letting stream export be measured as a whole-watershed output.
cards.quote: Their small-watershed approach used valleys on watertight bedrock that lets little water seep deep
cards.section: Pools, fluxes and residence time

cards.front: In the Hubbard Brook clear-cut experiment, the felled trees were left on site and herbicide kept regrowth down. Why, and what did stream nitrate do?
cards.back: Plant uptake fell sharply with no nutrients carried off in wood, against an uncut reference watershed. Stream nitrate export rose sharply; reduced plant uptake is the main expected contributor, but cutting and herbicide also changed drainage, temperature, moisture and microbes, so the rise is a combined effect.
cards.quote: The felled trees stayed on site and herbicide kept regrowth down, so plant uptake fell sharply with no nutrients carried off in wood
cards.section: Pools, fluxes and residence time

cards.front: Why can the Hubbard Brook clear-cut result not be attributed to loss of plant uptake alone?
cards.back: Cutting and herbicide also changed drainage, soil temperature and moisture, and microbial activity, so the nitrate rise is their combined effect.
cards.quote: Cutting and herbicide also changed drainage, soil temperature and moisture, and microbial activity, so the result is their combined effect, not uptake loss alone.
cards.section: Pools, fluxes and residence time

cards.front: After a forested watershed is cut, nitrate export in the stream rises sharply. Predict what happens to stream calcium export, and why.
cards.back: Calcium export rises too. Nitrate is a negative ion and drainage water stays electrically neutral, so positive ions such as calcium leave with it.
cards.quote: Nitrate is a negative ion and drainage water stays electrically neutral, so positive ions (cations) such as calcium leave with it
cards.section: Pools, fluxes and residence time

cards.front: A nutrient budget shows that a forest's nitrogen store fell. What can the budget show, and what can it not show?
cards.back: It shows that the store changed and through which boundary flux. It cannot show which process controls the system; that needs a causal test such as a whole-ecosystem experiment.
cards.quote: The rule is accounting: it shows that a store changed and through which boundary flux, not which process controls the system.
cards.section: Pools, fluxes and residence time

cards.front: Respiration by plants, animals and decomposers returns carbon to the air as CO2; on land, plants respire roughly as much as {{c1::decomposers}} do
cards.quote: Respiration by plants, animals and decomposers returns it as CO2; on land, plants respire roughly as much as decomposers do
cards.section: The carbon cycle: fast exchanges laid over slow stores

cards.front: Why does atmospheric CO2 in the Northern Hemisphere fall each summer and rise each winter?
cards.back: Photosynthesis and respiration run out of phase: in summer photosynthesis outpaces respiration and draws CO2 down; in winter respiration outpaces photosynthesis and CO2 rises.
cards.quote: In the Northern Hemisphere the two run out of phase: atmospheric CO2 falls each summer, when photosynthesis outpaces respiration, and rises each winter.
cards.section: The carbon cycle: fast exchanges laid over slow stores

cards.front: Why does the ocean hold far more carbon than the atmosphere?
cards.back: CO2 dissolved at the surface forms bicarbonate and carbonate, so seawater stores carbon in forms beyond dissolved CO2.
cards.quote: dissolved CO2 forms bicarbonate and carbonate, so the ocean holds far more carbon than the air.
cards.section: The carbon cycle: fast exchanges laid over slow stores

cards.front: Draw a boundary around the fast carbon cycle: air, ocean, plants and soil. Classify burning fossil fuel and photosynthesis as boundary fluxes or internal transfers.
cards.back: Burning fossil fuel is a boundary flux: it opens a large flux from a slow pool into the fast ones. Photosynthesis and respiration, however large, stay inside the line.
cards.quote: Left alone, fossil carbon is a pool with almost no outflow; burning it opens a large flux from a slow pool into the fast ones.
cards.section: The carbon cycle: fast exchanges laid over slow stores

cards.front: Using residence time = stock / flux, explain why fossil carbon left alone has an extremely long residence time, and what burning does to that residence time.
cards.back: Left alone, the pool has almost no outflow, so stock divided by a tiny flux is enormous. Burning adds a large outflow, so the same stock now drains on a far shorter timescale.
cards.why: Rests on residence time = stock / flux and on fossil carbon being a slow pool with almost no outflow.
cards.quote: Fossil carbon is organic matter buried over millions of years.
cards.section: The carbon cycle: fast exchanges laid over slow stores

cards.front: The atmosphere is about 78 percent N2. Why is that nitrogen out of reach of most organisms?
cards.back: The triple bond of N2 is hard to break; nitrogen fixers (some bacteria and archaea, with nitrogenase), lightning and fertiliser manufacture convert it.
cards.quote: The atmosphere is about 78 percent N2, but its triple bond puts it out of reach of most organisms.
cards.section: The nitrogen cycle: microbes run most of the transformations

cards.front: Nitrogen's oxidation state runs from {{c1::−3}} in ammonium through 0 in N2 to +5 in nitrate.
cards.quote: Nitrogen's oxidation state runs from −3 in ammonium through 0 in N2 to +5 in nitrate.
cards.section: The nitrogen cycle: microbes run most of the transformations

cards.front: What does nitrogen fixation do chemically, and which enzyme carries it out?
cards.back: It reduces N2 to ammonia, using nitrogenase. Some bacteria and archaea do it, free-living or in symbioses such as rhizobia in legume root nodules.
cards.quote: Fixation reduces N2 to ammonia, using the enzyme nitrogenase.
cards.section: The nitrogen cycle: microbes run most of the transformations

cards.front: Ammonification releases ammonium from organic nitrogen. Why is it not a redox step, unlike most nitrogen transformations?
cards.back: Nitrogen in organic matter and in ammonium is at the same oxidation state, so decomposers release it with no change in oxidation state.
cards.quote: Ammonification releases ammonium from organic nitrogen as decomposers break down dead matter, with no change in oxidation state
cards.section: The nitrogen cycle: microbes run most of the transformations

cards.front: What does nitrification do, and what does it require?
cards.back: It oxidises ammonia through nitrite to nitrate, and it requires oxygen. Classically ammonia oxidisers and nitrite oxidisers share the two steps.
cards.quote: Nitrification oxidises ammonia through nitrite to nitrate and requires oxygen.
cards.section: The nitrogen cycle: microbes run most of the transformations

cards.front: A well-drained soil becomes waterlogged and low in oxygen for weeks. Predict which nitrogen transformation is suppressed and which is favoured, and the effect on gas losses.
cards.back: Nitrification, which requires oxygen, is suppressed. Denitrification, which runs in low-oxygen soils, is favoured, reducing nitrate to gases such as NO, N2O and N2, so gaseous nitrogen losses can rise if nitrate is available.
cards.quote: Denitrification reduces nitrate or nitrite, in low-oxygen soils and sediments, to gases that can include NO, N2O and N2.
cards.section: The nitrogen cycle: microbes run most of the transformations

cards.front: For a boundary drawn around a watershed, classify each as input, output or internal: fixation, denitrification, nitrate leaving at the stream outlet, nitrification, plant uptake.
cards.back: Fixation is an input; denitrification and stream nitrate are outputs; nitrification and plant uptake are internal (the loop).
cards.why: Which steps cross the boundary depends on where the line is drawn.
cards.quote: For the watershed line, fixation is an input; denitrification and the nitrate leaving at the stream outlet are outputs
cards.section: The nitrogen cycle: microbes run most of the transformations

cards.front: What is anammox?
cards.back: Anaerobic ammonium oxidation: ammonium and nitrite are joined into N2 without oxygen (NH4+ + NO2− → N2 + 2 H2O), another gas output of fixed nitrogen.
cards.quote: One is anammox (anaerobic ammonium oxidation), which joins ammonium and nitrite into N2 without oxygen
cards.section: The nitrogen cycle: microbes run most of the transformations

cards.front: Anoxic seawater is given 15N-labelled nitrite and unlabelled ammonium. If anammox is the main route to N2, which N2 species should accumulate, and why?
cards.back: N2 with one 15N and one 14N. Anammox pairs one nitrogen from ammonium (14N here) with one from nitrite (15N), so doubly labelled N2 should not dominate.
cards.why: Rests on anammox joining one ammonium N and one nitrite N into N2 (NH4+ + NO2- -> N2 + 2 H2O).
cards.quote: in some oxygen-poor waters and sediments, denitrification is not the only biological route back to N2.
cards.section: The nitrogen cycle: microbes run most of the transformations

cards.front: What did the discovery of comammox in Nitrospira change about the textbook picture of nitrification?
cards.back: One organism can carry out complete ammonia oxidation to nitrate, so the two chemical steps need not belong to two groups of organisms.
cards.quote: so the two chemical steps of nitrification need not belong to two organisms
cards.section: The nitrogen cycle: microbes run most of the transformations

cards.front: Why can no organism fix phosphorus, and how does phosphorus mainly enter ecosystems?
cards.back: Phosphorus has no major gas, so there is nothing to pull from the air. It enters mainly as phosphate-bearing rock weathers.
cards.quote: Phosphorus has no major gas, so no organism can pull it from the air as nitrogen fixers pull N2.
cards.section: Phosphorus: the element no microbe can fix

cards.front: Much phosphorus ends in marine sediments. Over geological time, what is the main route back to land?
cards.back: Uplift of those sediments. Seabirds and fish migrating up rivers return a smaller amount.
cards.quote: over geological time, uplift of those sediments is the main route back to land
cards.section: Phosphorus: the element no microbe can fix

cards.front: Phosphorus is released from a lake's sediments into its water. Is that an input or an internal transfer?
cards.back: It depends on the boundary: internal if the line is drawn around water and sediments together, an input if it is drawn around the water alone.
cards.quote: phosphorus released from sediment is an internal transfer (around the water alone, it would be an input)
cards.section: Phosphorus: the element no microbe can fix

cards.front: A nutrient is {{c1::limiting}} when adding it on its own increases production.
cards.quote: A nutrient is limiting when adding it on its own increases production, and a lake rich in nutrients and dense with algae is eutrophic.
cards.section: Phosphorus: the element no microbe can fix

cards.front: A lake is divided into two basins. Both receive nitrogen and carbon; only one also receives phosphate. Why this design, and what does a bloom in only the phosphate basin show?
cards.back: The basins share weather and history, so phosphate is the only difference. A bloom only there shows phosphorus supply set algal biomass in that lake.
cards.why: A nutrient is limiting when adding it on its own increases production.
cards.quote: Collect years of pre-treatment data on it and on an untreated reference lake, then divide it, as in Lake 226.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A eutrophic lake has long received both nitrogen and phosphate. Managers stop the nitrogen additions but phosphate continues. Predict the algae and explain using the nitrogen and phosphorus budgets.
cards.back: The lake likely stays eutrophic, as nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria increase. Nitrogen has a boundary input phosphorus lacks, fixation from the air, so cutting nitrogen alone can fail while phosphorus supply continues.
cards.why: Rests on the budget rule plus phosphorus having no gas phase; this is the Lake 227 result.
cards.quote: But nitrogen has an input phosphorus lacks: fixation from the air.
cards.section: Phosphorus: the element no microbe can fix

cards.front: In a grassland addition experiment, nitrogen alone and phosphorus alone each leave production unchanged, but nitrogen plus phosphorus together raise it. How is this described?
cards.back: Co-limitation: production rises only when both nutrients are added together. Neither is limiting on its own by the strict definition.
cards.quote: Two nutrients co-limit production when it rises only if both are added together, a common result in nitrogen and phosphorus addition studies.
cards.section: What the second film left out

cards.front: An invented annual carbon budget gives emissions E = 10.0 GtC yr⁻¹, atmospheric accumulation A = 5.0, ocean sink O = 2.5 and land sink L = 2.0. What is the residual B, and what does a nonzero B mean?
cards.back: B = E − A − O − L = 10.0 − 5.0 − 2.5 − 2.0 = 0.5 GtC yr⁻¹. Some flux is unmeasured or misestimated, or errors exceed it; the budget does not close.
cards.quote: So a budget is only as good as its measured fluxes.
cards.section: What a budget can and cannot show

cards.front: A global carbon budget's residual comes out at exactly zero. Why does that not prove every term was measured well?
cards.back: The zero can come from rounding, single terms (the land sink) can carry uncertainty far larger than the residual, and errors in two terms can cancel.
cards.quote: Errors in two terms could cancel and still give zero.
cards.section: What a budget can and cannot show

cards.front: Name four common reasons nutrient budgets fail to close.
cards.back: Unmeasured fluxes; sampling frequency and record length; tracer bias; compensating errors.
cards.quote: Budgets often fail to close. Four common reasons: Unmeasured fluxes.
cards.section: What a budget can and cannot show

cards.front: Why is nitrogen lost by denitrification so often an unmeasured flux in budgets?
cards.back: The N2 it releases is hard to detect against an atmosphere that is already mostly N2.
cards.quote: N2 lost by denitrification is hard to detect against an atmosphere that is mostly N2.
cards.section: What a budget can and cannot show

cards.front: Nitrogen fixation is measured by adding 15N2 to water as a gas bubble. Why can this underestimate fixation, and how is it avoided?
cards.back: The bubble does not fully equilibrate with the water, so organisms see less tracer than assumed. Dissolve the 15N2 in water beforehand.
cards.quote: as a gas bubble, which does not fully equilibrate with water, can underestimate nitrogen fixation
cards.section: What a budget can and cannot show

cards.front: A watershed receives 12 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ in deposition and 3 from fixation; stream export is 5 and measured denitrification 2. Inventories a year apart show storage rose by 3 kg N ha⁻¹. What does the budget imply, and what could explain it?
cards.back: Predicted gain 15 − 7 = +8, observed +3, so about 5 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ is unaccounted for: an unmeasured output such as N2 loss, an overestimated input, or inventory error.
cards.why: change in stock = inputs − outputs; a budget is only as good as its measured fluxes.
cards.quote: N2 lost by denitrification is hard to detect against an atmosphere that is mostly N2.
cards.section: What a budget can and cannot show

cards.front: A forest on nitrogen-rich mica schist gains more nitrogen in inventories than measured deposition plus fixation minus outputs can explain. What unmeasured flux could close the budget?
cards.back: Rock weathering as an input: nitrogen-rich bedrock can supply nitrogen that a budget counting only atmospheric inputs misses.
cards.why: Rests on unmeasured fluxes as a cause of non-closure; rock can be an input.
cards.quote: Rock can be an input: weathering of nitrogen-rich mica schist supplied nitrogen at forest sites in the Klamath Mountains.
cards.section: What a budget can and cannot show

cards.front: A lake manager wants to know whether to control nitrogen or phosphorus to stop summer algal blooms. Why manipulate the whole lake rather than bottles of lake water, and what limits the answer?
cards.back: Bottles miss slow responses such as rising nitrogen fixation, sediment nutrient release and grazing changes. Use pre-treatment years, a reference lake and a divided lake. One lake is not a replicate, so repeat across lakes.
cards.quote: bottle experiments miss slow responses such as rising nitrogen fixation, nutrient release from sediments or changes in grazing
cards.section: Design problem
